Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)] is normally distributed. Then the probability density function [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: X] is a unimodal, bell-shaped curve. Moreover, it is symmetrical about the mean, median, and mode, which all equal [MATH: \mu].

Content:
We can use the normal distribution to model a wide range of real-life situations because many real-world distributions are roughly bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean value.

Content:

Content:
To determine whether a given data is normal, the first thing to do is to check the shape of the distribution. For example, if a data set is roughly bell-shaped, then it might be normally distributed.

Content:

Let [MATH: X] represent the weight of a randomly selected baby. Then we have [MATH: X \sim N(3\,543, 609^2).]

We want to find [MATH: P(3\,100 < X < 3\,600).] First, we convert [MATH: X] to a standard normal random variable by [MATH: z]-scoring:

[MATH: P(3100 < X < 3600)|= P((3100 − 3543)/(609) < Z < (3600 − 3543)/(609)); = P(− 0.73 < Z < 0.09)]

Now, we express the required probability in terms of [MATH: \Phi(z)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: P(− 0.73 < Z < 0.09)|= P(Z < 0.09) − P(Z < − 0.73); = P(Z ≤ 0.09) − P(Z ≤ − 0.73); = Φ(0.09) − Φ(− 0.73)]

From the table, we have the following:

[MATH: Φ(− 0.73)|= 0.2327; Φ(0.09)|= 0.5359]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: P(− 0.73 < Z < 0.09)|= Φ(0.09) − Φ(− 0.73); = 0.5359 − 0.2327; = 0.3032.]

In conclusion, the probability that a randomly selected newborn baby weighs more than [MATH: 3\,100] grams but less than [MATH: 3\,600] is [MATH: 0.30.]

[MATH: − (5)/(σ)|= − 0.8416; (1)/(σ)|= 0.1683; σ|= (1)/(0.1683); σ|≈ 6minutes.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)] is normally distributed. Then the probability density function [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: X] is a unimodal, bell-shaped curve. Moreover, it is symmetrical about the mean, median, and mode, which all equal [MATH: \mu].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4d4ba480e83412d48f48e90b734de427]

Content:
We can use the normal distribution to model a wide range of real-life situations because many real-world distributions are roughly bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean value.

Content:
Patients' blood pressures, people's weights, measurement errors, and IQ scores are just some of the real-world examples that can be modeled as a normal distribution.

Content:
To determine whether a given data is normal, the first thing to do is to check the shape of the distribution. For example, if a data set is roughly bell-shaped, then it might be normally distributed.

Content:
It should be noted that, in practice, statisticians will often need to perform several tests on the data to check for normality (these are called normality tests). We cannot rely only on a distribution's shape since other distributions are also bell-shaped. However, checking the shape is often a good starting point.

The birth weights of newborns in a given population are normally distributed with a mean of [MATH: 3\,543] grams and a standard deviation of [MATH: 609] grams. Explanation:
Let [MATH: X] represent the weight of a randomly selected baby. Then we have [MATH: X \sim N(3\,543, 609^2).]

We want to find [MATH: P(3\,100 < X < 3\,600).] First, we convert [MATH: X] to a standard normal random variable by [MATH: z]-scoring:

[MATH: P(3100 < X < 3600)|= P((3100 − 3543)/(609) < Z < (3600 − 3543)/(609)); = P(− 0.73 < Z < 0.09)]

Now, we express the required probability in terms of [MATH: \Phi(z)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: P(− 0.73 < Z < 0.09)|= P(Z < 0.09) − P(Z < − 0.73); = P(Z ≤ 0.09) − P(Z ≤ − 0.73); = Φ(0.09) − Φ(− 0.73)]

From the table, we have the following:

[MATH: Φ(− 0.73)|= 0.2327; Φ(0.09)|= 0.5359]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: P(− 0.73 < Z < 0.09)|= Φ(0.09) − Φ(− 0.73); = 0.5359 − 0.2327; = 0.3032.]

In conclusion, the probability that a randomly selected newborn baby weighs more than [MATH: 3\,100] grams but less than [MATH: 3\,600] is [MATH: 0.30.]
